title: IB Breakdown of Grades: 1-7 and 45-Point System
summary: Understand the IB breakdown of grades, including subject scores, core points, grade boundaries, diploma passing rules, and ways to improve results.
body_markdown:
The **IB breakdown of grades** has two connected parts. Each of the six Diploma Programme subjects receives a grade from **1 to 7** , while Theory of Knowledge (TOK) and the Extended Essay (EE) can contribute up to **3 additional points** . The maximum IB Diploma score is therefore **45 points** .


A total of **24 points** is necessary for the diploma, but it does not guarantee the award. Students must also complete Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS) and satisfy conditions involving individual grades, Higher Level (HL) points, Standard Level (SL) points, TOK, and the EE.


### IB breakdown of grades at a glance


The final diploma score combines six subject grades with the TOK and EE core points. CAS is compulsory but does not add numerical points.


Diploma component Grading system Maximum contribution


Six academic subjects Each subject graded 1-7 42 points


Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay Each graded A-E, then combined 3 points


Creativity, Activity, Service Completion requirement 0 points


**Maximum diploma total** Subjects plus core **45 points**


The calculation is:


**Six subject grades + TOK/EE core points = final IB Diploma score out of 45**


For example, HL grades of 6, 6, and 5 combined with SL grades of 5, 5, and 4 produce 31 subject points. If the student earns 2 core points, the final diploma score is **33** .


### Understanding the 1-7 IB subject grades


Every completed DP subject receives a final grade between **1 and 7** , with 7 representing the highest achievement. These grades are not percentages: a 7 does not mean 70%, and a 4 does not automatically mean 40%.


IB grade Broad level of achievement


**7** Excellent


**6** Very good


**5** Good


**4** Satisfactory


**3** Limited or mediocre


**2** Poor


**1** Very poor


These descriptions are broad. The IB's[official grade descriptors](https://ibo.org/contentassets/0b0b7a097ca2498ea50a9e41d9e1d1cf/dp-grade-descriptors-en.pdf) explain the expected quality of knowledge, analysis, evaluation, communication, and subject-specific skills.


A grade 4 is often treated as a practical benchmark, but the IB does not designate a universal passing grade for an individual DP course. The[IB assessment FAQ](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/getting-results/assessment-faq/) confirms that schools and universities may set their own requirements for admission, credit, or progression.


### How assessment marks become a subject grade


Most IB subjects contain several assessment components. Depending on the course, these may include examination papers, internal assessments, oral tasks, practical work, or externally assessed coursework.


The process normally follows four stages:


1. **Marks are awarded** using assessment criteria or a markscheme.
2. **Component marks are scaled** according to the weighting in the subject guide.
3. Scaled marks are combined into an **overall mark** .
4. That mark is compared with the session's **grade boundaries** to produce a grade from 1 to 7.


Exact weightings vary by subject, level, and curriculum version. Students should therefore use the guide and assessment model for their specific course rather than assuming that every internal assessment has the same value.


The IB uses both internally and externally assessed work. As explained in the[official assessment overview](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/understanding-ib-assessment/) , school-marked tasks may be moderated to keep standards comparable across schools.


### What IB grade boundaries mean


A **grade boundary** is the cut-off that converts an overall assessment mark into a subject grade. If a hypothetical grade 6 boundary is 68, a mark of 68 receives a 6, while 67 remains in the grade below.


There is no fixed percentage that always produces a particular grade. Boundaries can differ according to:


- subject and course level
- examination session
- assessment component
- syllabus or assessment model
- examination variant, where applicable


IB assessment is **criterion-related** , meaning performance is judged against established standards rather than determined by a simple ranking of classmates. Examiners and IB staff consider grade descriptors, marked student work, statistical evidence, examiner judgment, and teacher feedback when setting boundaries.


Boundaries may change when papers differ in difficulty. Their purpose is to preserve a comparable achievement standard, not to reward or penalize a cohort. The[RevisionDojo guide to IB grade boundaries](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-explained) explains the relationship between raw marks, scaled marks, and final grades.


Historical boundaries can help interpret mock results, but they do not predict future cut-offs. The[RevisionDojo IB Grade Calculator](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grade-calculator) can estimate grades when students select the correct subject, level, session, and available examination variant.


### Higher Level and Standard Level grades


HL and SL subjects both use the 1-7 scale. A grade 7 at SL contributes the same **7 diploma points** as a grade 7 at HL, although HL courses normally involve greater depth, breadth, and recommended teaching time.


For students taking the usual three HL and three SL subjects, at least **12 points across HL** and **9 points across SL** are required. If four HL subjects are registered, the three highest HL grades count toward the minimum. A student registered for two SL subjects needs at least **5 SL points** .


Universities may impose higher conditions, such as a specified overall total and particular HL grades. These admission requirements are separate from the IB's diploma award rules.


### TOK, the Extended Essay, and core points


TOK and the EE are each graded from **A to E** . Their grades are combined through the official core points matrix to contribute between 0 and 3 points.


Extended Essay / TOK A B C D E


**A** 3 2 2 2 Failing condition


**B** 2 2 2 1 Failing condition


**C** 2 2 1 0 Failing condition


**D** 2 1 0 0 Failing condition


**E** Failing condition Failing condition Failing condition Failing condition Failing condition


A B in TOK and a C in the EE earn 2 core points. Two D grades add no points but do not by themselves cause failure. An **E in either TOK or the EE is a failing condition** , regardless of the student's numerical total.


CAS is not graded from 1 to 7 or A to E. It contributes no points, but its requirements must be completed. The official[DP passing criteria and core points matrix](https://ibo.org/about-the-ib/what-it-means-to-be-an-ib-student/recognizing-student-achievement/about-assessment/dp-passing-criteria/) is the definitive reference.


### Requirements for passing the IB Diploma


Students need at least **24 total points** , but the diploma is not awarded if any of these conditions applies:


- CAS requirements have not been met.
- The total is below **24 points** .
- A required subject, TOK, or the EE has no grade awarded.
- TOK or the EE receives an **E** .
- Any subject receives a **grade 1** .
- A grade 2 is awarded in three or more subjects.
- A grade 3 or below is awarded in four or more subjects.
- The required HL or SL point total is not achieved.


A student could therefore exceed 24 points but fail because CAS is incomplete, the EE receives an E, or the HL total is too low. Students who complete individual courses without meeting every diploma condition receive **Diploma Programme course results** recording the grades awarded.


### Predicted grades compared with final grades


A **predicted grade** is a teacher's evidence-based estimate, often informed by mock examinations, timed assessments, coursework, and class performance. It is not an official final result.


Final grades are determined after assessed work has been marked, moderated where necessary, weighted, and converted using the applicable boundaries. The[RevisionDojo comparison of predicted and final grades](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/difference-between-ib-predicted-grades-and-final-results) explains why the two may differ. Reliable predictions should use several recent performances rather than one unusually strong or weak test.


### Using the grade breakdown to improve results


Effective planning begins with component-level evidence. Rather than recording only a total, students should classify lost marks as knowledge gaps, application errors, weak evaluation, misunderstood command terms, or timing problems.


A practical process is to:


- complete a timed paper or substantial section
- mark it with the relevant markscheme
- calculate performance by topic and question type
- identify components near the next boundary
- correct recurring weaknesses
- retest under similar conditions


Aim several marks above historical boundaries because future cut-offs are unknown. RevisionDojo's[IB subject resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib) can support targeted review, while[RevisionDojo Mock Exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-mock-exams) provide timed practice. Jojo AI and the Questionbank are most useful when students analyze errors rather than completing questions without reflection.


### Conclusion


The IB grading system combines six subject grades worth up to **42 points** with up to **3 core points** from TOK and the EE. Although **24 points** is the minimum total, students must also meet the individual-grade, HL, SL, core, and CAS conditions.


Use RevisionDojo's Grade Calculator to estimate current performance, then apply the Questionbank, Mock Exams, Study Notes, and Jojo AI to the weaknesses most likely to produce the next point.
